title: The Deepest Dive
objective: After this level you can describe the dives to the deepest point in the ocean.
summary: In 1960 Trieste, lifted by gasoline and sunk by iron, reached Challenger Deep. Cameron dove solo in 2012; Vescovo went down four times in 2019.

cards.headline: On January 23, 1960, two men sank to the deepest place in the ocean.
cards.body: Jacques Piccard and US Navy Lieutenant Don Walsh rode the bathyscaphe Trieste to the bottom of Challenger Deep, about 11 km down. Nobody went back to the bottom until 2012. How do you get down there, and home again?

cards.headline: A balloon in the sea
cards.body: Trieste hung from a huge float filled with gasoline. Gasoline is lighter than water, so it gave lift, and it barely compresses, so the deep couldn't crush the float the way it shrank Level 9's foam cup. To sink, Trieste carried heavy iron pellets held by electromagnets. To come home, it simply let them go.

cards.headline: Twenty minutes at the bottom
cards.body: The trip down took nearly five hours. Trieste reported about 10,916 m, the crew stayed about 20 minutes, then dropped ballast for a rise of more than three hours. HMS Challenger's rope had found 8,184 m there in 1875. Use Level 9's rule and divide by 10: the water was pressing with roughly 1,090 atmospheres.

questions.prompt: What did Victor Vescovo's Limiting Factor do at Challenger Deep in 2019 that no submersible had done before?

options.label: Made the first dive to the bottom
Made the first solo dive to the bottom
Measured the depth with a weighted rope
Reached the bottom more than once

questions.explanation: Between April 28 and May 5, 2019, Limiting Factor reached the bottom of Challenger Deep four times, a first for any submersible.

questions.prompt: Why was Trieste's float filled with gasoline rather than air?

options.label: Gasoline is lighter than water and barely compresses
Gasoline fueled its engines on the bottom
options.rationale: The gasoline was for lift, not fuel.

options.label: Air is heavier than seawater
options.rationale: Air is far lighter; the problem is that it compresses.

options.label: Gasoline kept the crew warm
options.rationale: It gave lift without being crushed.

questions.explanation: Gasoline floats on water but barely compresses, so it kept giving lift where pressure would have crushed air.

questions.prompt: Using Level 9's rule, about how many atmospheres did the water add at Trieste's 10,916 m?

options.label: About 10,916
options.rationale: That's the depth in meters, not atmospheres.

questions.explanation: Divide the depth in meters by 10: at about 10,916 m, the water adds roughly 1,090 atmospheres.
